sources.title: Learn about rent increases in San Francisco
sources.scope: Rent can be increased only once every 12 months; calculated on base rent only (incl. parking/storage, excl. temporary passthroughs); no rounding up; 30-day written notice (90-day if the increase, alone or combined in the same year, exceeds 10%); +5 days if mailed; notice should state dollar amount, percentage, effective date; rent increase license required (Housing Inventory); banking allowed; no extra rent charge merely for an additional occupant/roommate.

sources.publisher: City and County of San Francisco (SF.gov, Rent Board)
sources.title: Banked rent increases
sources.scope: A landlord may bank (save) an unused allowable increase and impose it later (banking allowed since April 1, 1982); no limit on amount banked; banked increases do not expire during a tenancy; new owners may use prior owners' bank; banked increases do not carry to a new tenant; not compounded or prorated - add the percentages, then multiply by current base rent; notice must state which part is banked; 30-day notice, 90-day if >10%.

Bond-measure and certain utility passthroughs use Rent Board worksheets.

sources.title: Civil Code section 827 - notice to change lease terms / rent
sources.scope: 827(b)(2): if the proposed increase is 10% or less of the rent charged at any time in the prior 12 months (alone or combined with other increases), notice at least 30 days before effective date; 827(b)(3)(A): if greater than 10%, at least 90 days; service by mail per Code of Civil Procedure 1013 (adds time).

sources.title: Civil Code section 1947.12 - Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482) rent cap
sources.scope: (a)(1): over any 12-month period rent may not increase more than 5% plus the percentage change in cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, measured from the lowest gross rental rate in the prior 12 months; (a)(2): no more than two increments in 12 months; (b): initial rent for a new tenancy is not capped (vacancy decontrol); (d)(3): section does not apply to housing subject to rent control through a public entity's valid police power that restricts annual increases below the state cap (i.e., stricter local rent control governs); (d)(5): single-family/condo exemption only if owner is not a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member.

sources.title: Civil Code section 1954.52 - Costa-Hawkins limits on local rent control
sources.scope: Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act (Ch. 2.7, secs. 1954.50-1954.535): local rent control may not apply to single-family homes or condominiums (separately alienable); a two-unit building (duplex) is not a single-family home for this purpose.

law_rows.rule: Residential units built on or before June 13, 1979 (and not single-family dwellings) have rent control and eviction protection under the SF Rent Ordinance (Admin. Code Ch. 37)

1.6% of base rent for increases effective March 1, 2026 - February 28, 2027 (60% of Bay Area CPI change; prior periods: 1.4% for 3/1/2025-2/28/2026, 1.7% for 3/1/2024-2/28/2025). Calculated on base rent only (includes parking/storage; excludes temporary passthroughs); increases cannot be rounded up
Rent may be increased only once every 12 months; the first annual increase may be imposed 12 months after the lease began; each later increase resets the anniversary date
The landlord must be current in the Rent Board Housing Inventory, which generates the rent increase license required before any annual or banked increase can take effect

Unused allowable increases may be banked and imposed later (banking allowed since April 1, 1982); no limit on the amount banked; banked amounts do not expire during a tenancy; they are added (not compounded or prorated) and multiplied by current base rent; new owners may use a prior owner's bank; banked amounts do not carry to a new tenant

30-day written notice for an increase of 10% or less (alone or combined with other increases in the same 12-month period); 90-day notice if more than 10%; add 5 days if the notice is mailed. The notice should state the dollar amount, the percentage, the effective date, and which part (if any) is banked
No additional rent may be charged simply because a new/additional roommate moves in with an existing tenant; that is an unlawful rent increase even if the lease allows it

Possible only through Rent Board processes: landlord petitions (capital improvement passthrough, operating & maintenance expense, comparable-rents special circumstances, Proposition I past rent history, utility passthrough) or Rent Board worksheets for bond/utility passthroughs; tenants do not pay petition-based increases until approved

There is no limit on the initial rent charged to a brand-new tenant of a vacant covered unit; the cap applies only to increases during an existing tenancy (both units here are occupied, so this does not apply now)

For units it covers: no more than 5% plus the regional cost-of-living change, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12 months, in at most two increments. It does NOT apply to housing already subject to a stricter local rent-control ordinance (1947.12(d)(3)) - so for this 1940 SF building the local 1.6% cap governs instead

Applies to all residential periodic tenancies regardless of rent control: at least 30 days' written notice if the increase is 10% or less of the rent charged at any time in the prior 12 months (alone or combined); at least 90 days if more than 10%; mail service adds time under CCP 1013

Local rent control cannot reach single-family homes or condos (separately alienable); a two-unit duplex is not a single-family home; vacancy decontrol is preserved statewide (1954.53). Corporate ownership matters only for the single-family/condo state-cap exemption (1947.12(d)(5)), not for a rent-controlled duplex

Unlawful to refuse to rent, or to discriminate in the terms, conditions, or privileges of rental (including rent amounts and increases), because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, or disability. HUD FHEO enforces it; complaints online, 1-800-669-9777, or mail; retaliation is illegal

law_rows.status: No federal statute capping residential rent increases was located on the official federal sources reviewed (U.S. Code / HUD). Federal law's role here is the Fair Housing Act's anti-discrimination rules; rent-amount limits come from state and local law

process_rows.requirement: Verify the building is rent controlled (year built on/before 6/13/1979 via the SF Property Information Map; no exemption) and that the Rent Board Housing Inventory is reported so a current rent increase license exists
Annual allowable increase (1.6% for 3/1/2026-2/28/2027) plus any properly banked increases; multiply the total percentage by base rent only; do not round up; only one increase per 12 months

Written notice personally delivered or mailed: at least 30 days before the effective date if the increase (alone or combined in the prior 12 months) is 10% or less; at least 90 days if more than 10%; add 5 days when mailed. State the dollar amount, percentage, effective date, and any banked portion

Keep the notice and calculation. Tenants can challenge an increase as unlawful at the Rent Board; free counseling at 415-252-4600; free legal help from the Eviction Defense Collaborative at 415-659-9184; discrimination/retaliation complaints go to the SF Human Rights Commission or HUD
The Rent Board's annual allowable increase (currently 1.6%) may be imposed once per 12 months without a petition - this is the normal, routine increase for a rent-controlled unit
Previously skipped allowable increases may be banked and added later; the notice must identify the banked portion
Capital improvement, operating & maintenance, comparable-rent, Proposition I, or utility passthroughs - only via Rent Board petition/worksheet before notice
Charging extra rent merely because an additional roommate moved in is an unlawful rent increase; any increase above the allowable amount without a successful petition is unlawful

practice_rows.topic: Do the same rules apply to big real-estate corporations and individual owners?
practice_rows.answer: For a rent-controlled duplex, yes: the SF Rent Ordinance applies to the landlord of a covered unit regardless of whether the owner is a corporation, LLC, or individual. The corporate-ownership distinction in California law (Civ. Code 1947.12(d)(5)) applies only to the single-family-home/condo exemption from the statewide AB 1482 cap, not to this building

practice_rows.topic: How corporations vs individual owners handle increases day to day
practice_rows.status: Unverified - blank. Operational habits (portfolio software, standardized notice letters, property managers) are business practices for which no official source exists; the legal obligations above are identical for both

practice_rows.topic: Raise one unit's rent or both?
practice_rows.answer: Applying the same lawful policy to both units is the normal, defensible practice: the same allowable percentage, computed on each unit's own base rent, with the same notice procedure for each. The federal Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to discriminate in the terms or conditions of a rental (including the amount of an increase) because of a protected class, so treating identical units differently without a neutral, documented, lawful reason (for example a different anniversary date) invites scrutiny. Raising only one unit is not automatically illegal, but uniform treatment of both units is the approach that passes review most cleanly

Unit 1 (lease start 2/1/2025, continuing tenancy 4/1/2026, $3,995/mo) and Unit 2 (lease start 6/1/2019, $3,150/mo, no increase since 2019) are both covered; each unit's increase is computed on its own base rent and anniversary timing. Unit 2 may also have banked increases available (amount blank pending the official 571 year-by-year list)

qa.question: What is a reasonable and normal rental increase for these units in 94122 under local, state, and federal law?
qa.answer: Local: the SF Rent Board annual allowable increase - 1.6% of base rent for 3/1/2026-2/28/2027 - once every 12 months, plus any banked increases; 1940 building is rent controlled. State: AB 1482's 5%+CPI/10% cap does not apply because stricter local rent control governs (1947.12(d)(3)); the state notice statute (Civ. Code 827) still applies. Federal: no rent cap; only the Fair Housing Act's ban on discriminatory terms applies.

qa.question: How do big real-estate corporations handle increases vs individual owners in San Francisco?
qa.answer: Legally the same Rent Ordinance rules apply to both for a rent-controlled building; the corporate distinction exists only in the state single-family/condo exemption. Day-to-day operational differences are business practice and are unverified here (see Flagged for Review).

qa.question: What is the correct way to inform tenants, and what are reasonable reasons?
qa.answer: Serve a written notice (30 days for increases of 10% or less combined over 12 months; 90 days above 10%; +5 days if mailed) stating the dollar amount, percentage, effective date, and any banked portion, after confirming the rent increase license via the Housing Inventory. Reasonable reasons: the annual allowable increase, banked increases, and Rent Board-approved passthroughs. Charging more for an added roommate is not allowed.

qa.question: Can the increase pass review by SF tenant advocates and free tenant lawyers?
qa.answer: A documented increase within the allowable cap, with correct notice and a current rent increase license, is the normal lawful practice. SF tenants have free counseling (Rent Board 415-252-4600) and free legal help (Eviction Defense Collaborative 415-659-9184); have a tenant lawyer review the notice and calculation before serving.

qa.question: Raise one unit's rent or both?
qa.answer: Raise both units under the same uniform policy (same allowable percentage on each unit's base rent, same notice procedure). Differential treatment of the two units without a neutral documented reason risks a fair-housing (disparate treatment) challenge under 42 U.S.C. 3604(b).
